The tumblers in the apartment door shifted as he turned the key, and set in place with a familiar click. It had been almost a month since he'd left his old job and opted to do freelance repair service. No more constantly patching up superhero-sized holes in the headquarters walls when trainees lost their tempers, no more pipe repairs when individuals accidentally froze over the men's room, and, perhaps best of all, no more having to replace every goddamn lightbulb (to say nothing of all the wiring, structural damage, tiling, and so on) when villains came calling. Maybe his life wasn't spectacular now, but it was pretty good, and that's all he had ever wanted.

Unfortunately for the organization of heroes, their non-hero employment proved to be anything but 'pretty good.' The pay was awful, as "serving heroes is its own reward," the benefits were lacking, and the job itself was a constant ordeal, as he had learned all too well over the years. Worse still, the government tended to look the other way where heroes broke minor laws, given that most served as the enforcers of the major ones. That was all fine and dandy for them, but without even minimal government supervision, abuses ran rampant in the workplace. Supervisors ignored safety regulations, cut corners wherever possible, and made life a living hell for any who objected. The corporate side began squeezing its workforce, insisting that the long hours and low pay contributed to a greater cause, and that compensation would be given when the headquarters could afford it, but that day never seemed to come. He would have left the week he started, but leaving the organization was taboo in the larger community. After all, who would voluntarily object to serving this noble cause?

The replacement for his colleague came as a shock to him. The day shift communications specialist was a veteran of the organization's behind-the-scenes work, and made it his job to take care of the poor bright-eyed individuals who signed on thinking the proximity to superheroes somehow justified the terrible working conditions, as he once did. He found a friend in him one day when the specialist needed a handyman to rewire a console. Despite his disgruntled nature, he took pride in the work he did, and he and the specialist found rapport with one another in being the 'true heroes' of the complex.

Throughout the years, there had been many attacks on headquarters, and everyone believed the lockdown drills had been pretty effective in protecting the most vulnerable employees in the complex. He couldn't recall the last death that had actually occurred on the grounds. The communications room itself, however, needed to be heavily fortified, the services provided too critical to allow the specialist to leave his post in an emergency. Thanks to the mismanagement of the complex, it remained as vulnerable a point in headquarters as it was the day the organization was founded. And over time, the villains learned that tidbit.

The specialist ended up dying in the line of duty, as their contracts stipulated might rarely happen, yet there were no grand memorials, no mournings, no opulent ceremonies, as heroes were wont to do for their own fallen comrades. A very quiet burial for the family, non-disclosure agreements to keep the grieving silent, and a new opening for a communications specialist. Though deaths were relatively rare, other support staff who had fallen as a result of collateral damage had been treated much the same way, bodies disposed of quietly, fresh job postings popping up, to protect the safe image projected by the organization. Had the specialist's family not informed him of his friend's untimely death, he might have believed the misleading retirement-and-protection-program story the public relations division had woven.

He quit the day he found out. He told everybody he could in the complex: His own disclosure clauses did not extend to the other employees, and whether he endeavored to spite his masters, avenge his friend, or attempt to save the lives of his coworkers, it didn't matter. The news inevitably spread outside the complex, and the effects of a more informed populace were catastrophic. Some left, some stayed, some even tried to unionize. The city began to protest the organization, and the corporate arm knew they had done themselves in. He didn't stick around for the aftermath. He'd had enough of these 'heroes', after what had happened. Or so he thought.

You know, it's funny. If I were born thirty years ago, I might have identified with that political party at some point. Everybody here talks about the self-reliance remarks as a cynical joke, but in the 70s and 80s, it very well would have been possible to walk into a restaurant, or a mechanic, or whatever, and pick up a trade, learn the skills, and turn that into a viable living. I'd imagine that was due in part to the availability of the factory jobs that people in certain regions so fondly remember. But globalization changed the face of the workplace in the country forever, and technology moves ever forward, increasing the ratio of productivity to human labor.

It's no longer possible to bring those jobs back simply because it's cheaper to outsource. If tariffs and/or tax cuts are introduced to try and bring those jobs back, depending on wages, manufacturers may find it more cost-effective to invest in automation, and like I said, the technology is constantly improving. I hear the counterarguments that say "New jobs will appear to support the automation," and they're not wrong, but 

a) there probably won't be nearly as many support positions to counteract the loss of labor positions automation causes, (else, what's the point of automation?) and 

b) the people replaced won't necessarily be able to do the jobs automation creates.

So that leaves us at a sobering question, "What happens to the unemployable?" It's a question I fear will have an unpleasant answer, with the current state of affairs.
